issues.issue: Optionor's duty to bear "all costs" for traffic studies sits against Section 12's later statement that costs reimbursable under Act 381 are the responsibility of Optionee or its Developer.

"Optionee will use its best efforts to secure funds to reimburse" promises effort toward obtaining funding rather than payment, and neither "best efforts" nor "reasonable documented expenses" is defined or benchmarked.

The clause creates an Optionee obligation that arises precisely when the Developer does not purchase, which is hard to square with Section 14's provision that on non-exercise the Option terminates "without further action or obligation on the part of either party."
"Support and written consent when required" does not say by whom or in what circumstances consent is "required," leaving the trigger for the duty open.

Optionor is to draft the Brownfield Plan, while Section 8 and the next sentence place the determination and costing of Eligible Activities on Optionee, leaving overlapping responsibility for the same document.
"Reasonable and necessary to affect Optionee's intended use" both uses "affect" for "effect" and supplies no standard for judging the estimates, and it does not say who decides.

The phrase "obtain approval of the Brownfield Plan for the project prior to Optionee by no later than December 1, 2006" is garbled; "prior to Optionee" has no object and the sentence's requirement cannot be read straight.

The deadline may be extended by the Optionor "so long as the delays are not caused by the Optionor," giving the party whose fault disables the extension the unilateral power to declare it, with no test of causation.

"That amount" has two possible referents — the amount the City approved or the shortfall below the agreed Eligible Activity costs — and the deduction from the Outstanding Balance differs greatly depending on which is meant.
It borrows the "Limitation of Liability" cap defined in Section 8 for a different trigger (City approval shortfalls, not unapproved Due Care), without saying whether one $500,000 cap covers both.
"Any costs or expenses which may or will be reimbursed" under Act 381 is open-ended — "may" sweeps in anything potentially reimbursable — so the allocation it makes has no ascertainable boundary.
Read broadly it would shift back to Optionee the street-vacation and traffic-study costs that earlier paragraphs of Section 12 expressly place on Optionor.

Retention of the Outstanding Balance by Optionee cannot easily be squared with Section 3, under which that balance is never held by Optionee but is paid over time out of TIF reimbursements received by the Developer.

Free assignability "without the consent of the Optionor" is broader than Section 1, which makes the Option assignable "to Optionee's developer," and sits against the next sentence's consent requirement for further assignment.
The clause is triggered only if Optionee "elects not to exercise," saying nothing about mere lapse of the term, and "the rights, option, or fee simple interests granted herein" mixes categories.

Termination "without further action or obligation on the part of either party" cannot be squared with Section 12's promise that if the Developer does not purchase, Optionee will use best efforts to reimburse up to $50,000 of traffic-study costs.
"Do all acts as may be necessary to implement and effectuate the intent" is an open-ended further-assurances duty whose content is set only by the drafters' unstated "intent" and "general purpose."
Requiring all such documents to be "satisfactory to the parties and their respective counsel" gives each side an unmeasured veto that could swallow the further-assurances duty in the same section.

The sentence first names three documents (this Option, Exhibit 1 and the Memorandum) as the only agreements, then states that all undertakings are embodied in "this Option and Exhibit 1," dropping the Memorandum.

"Except as provided in the Act, all disputes ... shall be resolved under this Act" is circular: the carve-out and the rule point to the same statute, leaving unclear which disputes fall outside the Act's procedures.

The deemed-receipt rule (two business days after mailing, one after courier deposit) is hard to reconcile with Section 2, which makes exercise effective "on the date of the receipt of notice," and no rule is given for personal delivery.
A strict time-is-of-the-essence rule is in tension with Section 2's open-ended "not less than one (1) year" term and with the unilateral extension rights in Sections 2 and 12.

The clause provides only for a corporate resolution or, if Optionor is a partnership, general-partner approval, yet the preamble identifies Optionor as a Michigan limited liability company, so no listed document fits.
"Such other instruments as the Optionee shall deem appropriate in its reasonable judgment" leaves the required deliverables entirely to one party's judgment, with "reasonable" the only limit.
The recorded Memorandum describes the Property as "containing 10.89 acres" per Attachment A, while Section 1 of the Option says "approximately 10.89 acres" as described in Exhibit 1.

The recorded statement that the Option "is fully assignable ... to Optionee's developer" is narrower than Section 13, which allows assignment by Optionee without Optionor's consent and without naming a Developer.
"Shall continue in effect for a period of not less than one (1) year" fixes a minimum but no expiration date, so the recorded term of the Option has no ascertainable end.
